[📃 PAPER ALERT] Efficient, Property-Aligned Fan-Out Retrieval via RL-Compiled Diffusion - by Google Research & UIUC
arXiv: https://t.co/tt5pGCsbU3

When we search something broad like “camping gear,” we don't really want 10 slightly different tents.

We want:
tent + sleeping bag + stove + headlamp + other complementary things.
So modern search systems use query fan-out: take one broad query --> generate multiple sub-queries --> retrieve different aspects of the user's intent.

Sounds simple.

But there is a problem.

LLMs are autoregressive. To generate a good set of complementary, diverse AND database-grounded queries, they may need expensive inference-time reasoning.

And for a search system... do we really want the model to “think” heavily every single time someone searches?

I think NO.

This paper proposes : Retrieve-for-Train.

The idea is actually quite interesting:

Use expensive RL during TRAINING, not during INFERENCE.

The pipeline has 3 stages:

Train a Fan-Out Language Model (FOLM) using RL to generate useful sub-queries.

The reward jointly optimizes:

a. Groundedness: are the queries actually connected to items in the database?
b. Alignment: do they still follow the user's original intent?
c. Diversity: do they explore genuinely different semantic directions?

Use this RL-trained model to generate synthetic supervision.
So the expensive exploration happens offline.
No human-labelled property-aligned dataset is required.

Train a lightweight diffusion retriever on these generated targets.

At inference time, instead of autoregressively generating query after query...

the diffusion model generates multiple retrieval directions in parallel in embedding space.

Basically:

RL discovers the search strategy --> synthetic data stores it --> diffusion executes it cheaply.

Findings:
1. Zero-shot query fan-out helps, but it is not enough.
Normal LLMs often generate near-identical queries.
R4T instead learns complementary directions that cover more of the semantic space.
2. R4T improves retrieval quality over zero-shot fan-out and Best-of-N baselines.
The method was evaluated on fashion and music retrieval tasks where the desired output is a set rather than one correct item.
3. The diffusion retriever makes fan-out dramatically cheaper.

Their 53.9M-parameter diffusion model generates the retrieval directions non-autoregressively.

Reported fan-out latency:

LLM: ~1.46 s → ~50 s as batch size grows
Diffusion: ~0.07 s → 4.21 s

That is roughly 12×–20× faster.

[Interestingly]
The diversity reward is doing something more important than simply making the results diverse.

Without it, the RL model can reward-hack.

Optimizing only groundedness can produce nonsense strings that happen to land close to database embeddings.
Adding alignment alone can instead make the model collapse into repetitive paraphrases.

Groundedness + Alignment + Diversity work like counter-anchors that prevent these shortcuts.

I found this part particularly interesting because it shows how important reward interaction is in RL-based retrieval.

[In short] Instead of asking a large model to solve the same difficult search problem again and again at inference time...solve it during training and compile the learned behavior into a smaller model.

So the idea is almost:
System-2-like exploration during training → System-1-like retrieval during deployment.
And I think the broader idea may be even more interesting than retrieval itself.
Can we use RL to discover expensive behaviors once, turn those behaviors into training data, and then deploy a much cheaper model that reproduces them?

**Holding AI to the Truth: Why Blockchain Matters** (written with assistance from @Grok.  

Artificial intelligence is extraordinary at producing fluent answers. It is less reliable at producing *settled* ones. On occasion — more often than casual users admit — models *hallucinate*: they invent citations, invent facts, invent confidence. The output can look authoritative and still be wrong. That is not a moral failing of the machine; it is a property of probabilistic generation without a shared ledger of what actually happened.

In July 2019, on Real Vision with Raoul Pal (@RaoulGMI) macro investor Dan Tapiero (@DTAPCAP) named the other half of this problem years before “AI agents” entered every pitch deck. Bitcoin, he argued, is not merely a coin. It is an *invention* — and at its core, “a truth machine”: a system bought for “certainty, of confirmation, of validity, of security,” a platform with a track record that makes fraud and silent revision harder. He later sharpened the phrase to “security truth machine.” (Popular memory sometimes upgrades that to “automatic truth machine”; the idea is the same.)

The distinction that matters for AI is precise. A blockchain does not magically know whether a claim about the physical world is true. It does not replace science, journalism, or judgment. What it *does* provide is **immutable, shared state**: who signed what, who paid whom, which model version ran, which data hash was used, which action an agent took and when. Once written under consensus rules, that record is extremely hard for any single party — including an AI system acting on someone’s behalf — to rewrite quietly.

That is exactly the property generative models lack. An LLM can narrate a trade that never settled, a contract that was never signed, a medical note that was never reviewed. An agent economy that scales without rails for settlement, identity, and audit is an economy of plausible fiction at machine speed. Tokenized dollars, on-chain credentials, and programmable settlement are not crypto fashion statements in that frame; they are **truth infrastructure for machine actors**.

Tapiero’s 2019 insight travels forward cleanly into the AI decade. The internet digitized information. Crypto digitizes value *and* verifiable record. If artificial intelligence is going to operate as a participant in markets, payments, and institutions — not merely as a chatbot — then “holding AI to the truth” cannot mean hoping the next model is nicer. It means binding machine action to ledgers that do not hallucinate their own history.

Blockchain is not the answer to every truth. It is the answer to a narrower, more urgent one: **who did what, with what authority, and can anyone erase the receipt?** In a world of confident machines, that receipt is not optional.

—
*Source: Tapiero × Raoul Pal, Real Vision “The Future of Macro Investing” (~Jul 2019), ~00:09:46 — “What it really is, is it’s a truth machine.” https://t.co/JxTkN4pGjO*

The guy who helped ship ChatGPT just said that same paradigm is why AI still can't automate real work.

Diogo Almeida spent years at OpenAI building the human-feedback techniques behind InstructGPT and ChatGPT. 

He left in 2024 to start TypeSafe AI. They just shipped their first product: a new model class called System One Models, and its first public model, Jev.

His bet: LLMs are trained on human preference and generate strings one token at a time. Great for chat. 

Bad for software, strings have to be parsed and validated before code can trust them, and there's always a chance the model goes off the rails.

Jev drops strings entirely.

→ Outputs typed, structured values instead of text — the schema is defined in advance, so type errors are mathematically impossible
→ Generates every output in parallel instead of token-by-token, so there's nothing to hallucinate into
→ Runs end-to-end in 70-500ms vs. 3-329 seconds for frontier LLMs
→ Costs $0.042 per million input tokens, output is free
→ Trained with a new method they call RLCD- optimized for calibrated probabilities on decisions, not for what a human rater would approve of

This isn't a ChatGPT competitor. It's not built for conversation at all. It's built to sit inside software and make the thousands of small, fuzzy decisions (classify, route, score, extract) that current LLMs are too slow, too expensive, and too unpredictable to run at scale.

🇬🇧 🏺 A 1,700-year-old Roman mystery

The dodecahedron found at Norton Disney in England is a bronze object with 12 faces, differently sized holes and small knobs at its corners. It was deposited around 1,700 years ago, yet no known Roman text or image explains what it was made for. More than a hundred similar objects have been discovered across the northwestern Roman Empire, leading to theories involving measurement, games, craftsmanship and rituals. The lack of clear wear patterns or inscriptions makes a specific function difficult to establish. Recent research has also explored possible symbolic meanings. Its rarity may be one of the most useful clues, showing that not every Roman artifact fits the practical categories modern observers expect. For now, the dodecahedron remains an object whose meaning has to be reconstructed from archaeological evidence rather than a definitive answer.
